title: Wallabies star Jordan Petaia’s future uncertain after suffering a season-ending shoulder injury
subtitle: A Reds star might have played his last match for Queensland after suffering a shoulder injury set to sideline him for the rest of the Super Rugby Pacific season.
content:
Jordan Petaia’s Super Rugby Pacific season is over, and so too could be his Queensland Reds career.
The Wallabies excitement machine is set to have surgery after dislocating his shoulder in the Reds’ 31-0 win over the Highlanders last Friday at Suncorp Stadium.
“We’ll get some finalisation of it but it looks like it will be a season-ending (injury),” Queensland coach Les Kiss said on Tuesday.
“Hopefully he’s all right by the end of the season and he can do some more things then (for the Wallabies).”
However, that remains uncertain, as does the off-contract Petaia’s future with the Reds.
He has reportedly been linked not only with moves to clubs in Europe and Japan, but also with a switch of codes, with NRL outfit St George Illawarra a reported potential destination.
“Those are (contract) conversations with RA (Rugby Australia) but we’d like to ensure he stays around,” Kiss said.
“He’s a good rugby player. He’s obviously disappointed (to be injured), but … once he’s got a pathway he can move forward and go from there.”
Kiss said Petaia’s loss was a blow for the Reds, who are also currently without suspended Wallabies pair Tate McDermott and Fraser McReight, as well as injured lock Seru Uru (thumb).
“His (Petaia’s) physical size and power is good, (and) when you couple that with also losing Fraser, Tate, Seru, there are some good players that are out, but I’ll just go back to the weekend (against the Highlanders) – some boys stood up,” the Reds coach said.
Kiss’ men, who have a 50 per cent record after eight matches, face a much tougher task on Saturday night at Suncorp Stadium against the second-placed Blues from Auckland.
“I know we’ve got certainly a different challenge this week but the young fellows stood up and did a great job (last Friday),” he said.
Kiss called for the Reds-Blues clash to become an Anzac round “tradition”.
“I think we played them last year in the same fixture and it’d be great to create a similar fixtures against the Blues on a year on basis and create that tradition,” Kiss said.
“It’s not missed on our boys. The research that’s gone into it adds depth and understanding to something bigger than the game.
“It’s going to be a special day and the (commemorative) jersey that’s been created, the boys love it, and I’m sure it’ll be fought in the spirit of respect of the past.”

title: Queensland Reds centre Josh Flook to return from a shoulder injury in Anzac round battle with Blues
subtitle: While Jordan Petaia will miss the rest of the Super Rugby Pacific season, one of his Queensland Reds teammates will return for Saturday’s clash with the Blues.
content:
Josh Flook will make a timely return from a shoulder injury to start at outside centre for the Queensland Reds on Saturday night against the Blues at Suncorp Stadium.
With Wallabies star Jordan Petaia ruled out for the rest of the Super Rugby Pacific season after dislocating his shoulder in the Reds’ 31-0 thrashing of the Highlanders last Friday, Flook’s return to the centres is a boost for the Queenslanders.
In one other backline change, Junior Wallabies winger Tim Ryan will make his starting debut for the Reds, replacing winger Mac Grealy, who has been left out of the 23-man match-day squad as part of “workload management”.
“I’m excited for the opportunity,” Ryan said.
“Just getting involved to make myself an option as often as possible is probably the most important thing I’ve learnt.”
There is also a change in the forwards, with lock Angus Blyth starting in place of Cormac Daly, who is nursing “injury niggles”.
The Reds are chasing their fifth win of the season but face a tough Anzac round challenge against the second-placed Blues, who demolished the ACT Brumbies by 39 points in Auckland last Saturday.
Queensland coach Les Kiss said: “We know the task ahead of us on Saturday. We’ve got to put forward our best team performance because the Blues were fairly compelling with what they did to the Brumbies last weekend.
“The Blues are a very good team. The fact we’ve done OK against a couple of New Zealand teams this season is good but this is a different kettle of fish.”
Blues coach Vern Cotter is wary of the Reds on their home soil.
“We’re under no illusion as to how difficult it’s going to be to play them up there in Queensland,” Cotter said.
“We’re playing on their turf and we feel they’ve simplified their game, looking to come at us reasonably direct on Saturday.
“They’re a team that defensively are quite good at holding players up and they’ll try to slow our ball down, so we’ve had an emphasis on ensuring we deal with that this week.
“We need to make sure we can get fast ball, and if we can I think we can create breaches and hopefully do enough damage to come away with the win.”

title: Super Rugby: Wallaby goes down as Reds romp to huge shutout win
subtitle: A Wallabies star went down while another did his international hopes no harm to inspire the Reds to a big shutout win against the Highlanders.
content:
In-form Reds centre Jordan Petaia left the field with a dislocated shoulder injury as Queensland midfielder Hunter Paisami shone in a fine Wallabies audition to inspire the Reds to a 31-0 victory at Suncorp Stadium over the Highlanders. 
Inside centre Paisami was excellent, scoring a try, setting up two more, and defending the lights out as he impressed with a deft kicking game that saw the Highlanders crash to their fifth consecutive loss.
But the all-round brilliance of Paisami, who scored the first try of the night and set up the last, was tempered by the worrying sight of ace utility back Petaia- who shifted from the wing to centre - leaving the game in the 33rd minute.
Petaia had his shoulder popped back in place on the field and his dislocated shoulder will likely have him out for the remainder of the season.

title: Tom Lynagh to miss Queensland’s clash with the Crusaders due to a hamstring injury
subtitle: The Reds have lost a key member of their side but will welcome back a Wallabies flanker for their clash with the Crusaders.
content:
Less than a week after catching the eye of new Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt, Reds flyhalf Tom Lynagh has succumbed to a hamstring injury and will miss Queensland’s battle with the Crusaders in Christchurch on Saturday.
Schmidt said Lynagh “did really well” in the Reds’ 41-34 Super Rugby Pacific loss to the Blues at Suncorp Stadium last Saturday night.
However, the 21-year-old son of Wallabies great Michael Lynagh has suffered an untimely injury setback and also seems likely to miss the Reds’ clash with the Melbourne Rebels on Friday week, despite Queensland coach Les Kiss saying the hamstring problem was “nothing major”.
“We hope it’s only two weeks maximum,” Kiss said.
Replacing Lynagh in the Queensland No.10 jersey will be Lawson Creighton.
“We have got options … so there’s no use risking someone if we don’t need to,” Kiss said.
“Lawson is a very well-organised player with a strong kicking game. We are very comfortable with him leading from No.10.”
Creighton’s inclusion is one of four changes to Queensland’s starting team.
Wallabies flanker Fraser McReight returns from suspension at the expense of John Bryant, 
prop Peni Ravai has been called into front-row in place of Alex Hodgman, and returning winger Mac Grealy starts in place of Suliasi Vunivalu, with Tim Ryan holding his wing spot after his three-try performance against the Blues.
“Tim Ryan put forward a compelling case to start again,” said Kiss, who added that McReight’s return was “fantastic”.
Centre Hunter Paisami will make his 50th appearance for the Reds.
“Hunter has been exceptional for us … the way he has grown his game,” Kiss said.
“He obviously carries hard but he’s also showing his skill at first and second receiver.
“His kicking has been impeccable and he’s also leading from the front with his experience.”
The Crusaders have won only two from nine this year, but the sixth-placed Reds won’t take a complacent attitude into the contest.
“Every team would be very wary of what the Crusaders can offer,” Kiss said.
“We are going to one of the great places in the world to play rugby and we will take on the challenge.”
 Peni Ravai, Matt Faessler, Jeffery Toomaga-Allen, Ryan Smith, Angus Blyth, Liam Wright, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson, Kalani Thomas, Lawson Creighton, Mac Grealy, Hunter Paisami, Josh Flook, Tim Ryan, Jock Campbell. 
 George Bower, Brodie McAlister, Fletcher Newell, Scott Barrett, Quinten Strange, Cullen Grace, Ethan Blackadder, Christian Lio-Willie, Mitch Drummond, David Havili, Sevu Reece, Dallas McLeod, Levi Aumua, Johnny McNicholl, Leigh Halfpenny.

title: Super Rugby: A star is born, but hat trick not enough for the Reds
subtitle: A superstar was born at Suncorp Stadium when Queensland Reds winger Tim Ryan scored three epic tries in a seesawing starting debut, but it wasn’t enough for the home side.
content:
A superstar was born at Suncorp Stadium when Queensland Reds winger Tim Ryan scored three epic tries in a seesawing starting debut which the home side lost 41-34 against the Blues.
Ryan was the star of the show, and did not deserve to be on the losing side. But in the dying moments, the Reds were their worst enemies, fumbling a 34-27 lead with five minutes left, and then collapsing in the final minute of play when two errors cost them a shot at bonus point with the scores level at 34-apiece.
With the clock dwindling down and an opportunity to claim victory in extra time looming, Louis Werchon pushed a long pass to reserve lock Joe Brial, who fumbled the ball. 
From there, the Blues went 40m through All Blacks winger Caleb Clarke before he found matchwinning scrumhalf Sam Nock, who broke the hearts of Queensland on the hooter with a crowd-silencing five-pointer. Suliasi Vunivalu coming in off his wing was the Reds second fatal mistake which starved them another chance to win the game.
“It’s what we expected coming here to Brisbane, a hostile environment, good side on their given day,” game winner Nock told Stan Sport.
“We had to grind for that right down to the last try.
“We were our own worst enemies at times (in the first half).”
Reds No.8 Harry Wilson said his side “let that slip” after Ryan had stamped his mark on the biggest stage.
“That was amazing from Tim Ryan,” Wilson said of the ‘junk yard dog’ who “goes 100 per cent” at training. 
“We saw the way he played tonight, It’s no surprise. He has done it at every level he has played and he was a game changer for us tonight.”
Ryan’s tries were not just normal tries scored by your typical winger, they were exciting, fantastic finishes only players with raw talent could produce.
His first was a 50m sprint off the Hunter Paisami assist, his second an incredible finish in the left corner and his third a piece of brilliance.
Halfback Louis Werchon attacked the blindside with a white hot Ryan, with flames steaming off his boot, on his left.
Finally when Ryan got the ball, he stepped inside and quickly back outside to completely bamboozle Taufa Funaki with a step 16325 vocal rugby fans had to have enjoyed.
From there, the 20-year-old junior Wallaby who attended St Patrick’s College Shorncliffe, had the pace and footwork to evade last line defender Cole Forbes to land his third try.
The only other time a Reds player has scored a hattrick was speed demon ‘Rocket’ Rod Davies against the Blues in the 2011 semi final.
“I told the guys at the end there I think they did the jersey justice and the occasion justice,” Reds co-captain Liam Wright told Stan Sport following an Anzac weekend spectacle at The Cauldron. 
20-year-old quicksilver winger Tim Ryan made his Super Rugby Pacific starting debut on Saturday night and his three try barrage indicates he is a future star.
From just one play where Ryan scooped up loose ball, regained his own chip kick, and found Brothers club mate Josh Flook on his right, Reds supporters saw enough to be excited.
Ryan, who had come in for Mac Grealy to have a rest, has something you can’t teach and that is pace. He is an elusive player, of immense potential.
Before last year’s StoreLocal Hospital Cup grand final between Brothers and Wests, then Brothers coach Brendan Gabbett said this of Ryan prior to his team’s grand final victory.
‘I don’t doubt that he could be a Wallaby. If we do the right thing with Tim Ryan as a code … Let him play week-in-week-out he could be a Wallaby that makes a difference not just a Wallaby.”
Indeed the lightweight young gun, who weighs 84 kilograms, showed that Wallaby potential during his starting debut for Queensland.
The last time he scored three tries in a game was a four try haul against Padua College as a Year 12 student playing AIC schoolboy rugby.
If Ryan’s ambitious chip and chase in the first half wasn’t impressive enough, his 50m try in the second half, the Reds second try in two minutes, had to be enough.
The Reds trailed 13-6, before a Suliasi Vunivalu try and a stunning Ryan try, orchestrated by in form centre Hunter Paisami who regained his own chip kick and unloaded to Ryan, turned the match on its head.
In less than three minutes, the Reds turned a 13-6 deficit into a 19-13 lead with 28 minutes left in the contest.
Ryan and hardworking No.8 Harry Wilson then combined to produce a trysaver on Blues forward battleship Hoskins Sototu moments later.
The livewire winger was everywhere in an 11-try bonanza at Suncorp.
The Waratahs face a huge challenge to make the Super Rugby finals after being beaten by bogey team the Chiefs 38-22 at Allianz Stadium on Friday night.
It marked the eighth consecutive occasion that the New Zealanders from Waikato have beaten NSW in a Super Rugby clash and heading into the latest showdown the winning margin was an average 22.1 points. 
The Waratahs now find themselves with two wins, seven losses and another five rounds left before the play-offs.
After the Force play the Highlanders on Saturday, NSW are set to drop to 11th spot on the table. That is the scenario after the Crusaders shock 39-0 thrashing of the Rebels in Friday’s early game.
The Waratahs showed what they are capable of with an impressive the first 20 minutes when they raced to a 12-0 lead. But by halftime the Chiefs had levelled the scores at 12-all. 
After the break the Chiefs unleashed and showed why they are such a threat in this competition.
“It was really fast and really physical at the start,” said Waratahs centre Lalakai Foketi.
“We knew they would come out swinging and we wanted to match that.
“I thought our first 30 was really good, but we couldn’t maintain it.
“It was really frustrating … we knew they were going to use their backs and we knew what was coming.” 
Waratahs skipper Jake Gordon said the first 40 minutes was a good battle.
“I thought we controlled field position, I thought we were getting confidence through our maul.” he said.
“The second half probably wasn’t as consistent, we turned pill over in the wrong side of the field and we allowed their backs to get quality ball and they were too good.”
Gordon said the Waratahs needed to find a way to get into the Chiefs territory a bit more in the second half.
“We knew how dangerous they were with the ball so it was a balance with giving them possession and also defending well, so we probably got the balance wrong in the second half,” he said. 
And the Waratahs’ campaign only gets tougher in the next two weeks as they face the table-topping Hurricanes in Wellington and third-placed Brumbies in Sydney. 
They then take on the Force in Perth, who have been revitalised following the addition of star new recruit Kurtley Beale. 
Waratahs winger Mark Nawaqanitawase, who was prominent in his return to the side, believes the team is still very much in race for the Super Rugby finals.
“100 per cent,” he said. “Each week we have to show up no matter who it is.
“That first half was 12-all, if we just held on for another 40 and we’d come away with a win” 
The Waratahs were up against it from kick-off on Friday with seven of their 10 contracted frontrowers unavailable for the game, including Wallabies prop Angus Bell whose presence makes such a difference to the team. 
“I’ve never had a cluster of injuries in a positional group like this before,” coach Coleman lamented.

title: Rugby Australia announces financial loss of more than $9 million
subtitle: Last year’s World Cup proved to be an extremely costly exercise for Rugby Australia.
content:
Rugby Australia has announced a $9.2 million loss for 2023, with the World Cup being blamed as the main reason for the major deficit.
It comes just a year after the RA made a profit of $8.2 million. 
Operating costs for 2023 were $11.5 million due to the World Cup, which proved to be a costly exercise for no rewards after the Wallabies failed to progress to the knockout stages of the tournament in France. 
However, the loss was less than those from the previous two World Cup years of 2019 ($9.5 million) and 2015 ($9.8 million).
RA chief executive officer Phil Waugh admitted 2024 would also be a financial battle for the sport’s national governing body, which is currently keeping the Melbourne Rebels afloat.
“From a revenue perspective 2024 will be another challenging year given we have had to take on the unplanned cost of the Melbourne Rebels’ operations for 2024, as well as additional investments and distributions to member unions, Super Rugby clubs, the community game, pathways and women’s rugby,” Waugh said.
However, Waugh said there was a “clear path forward” in terms of “uniting the game from the grassroots to the elite level”.
“We could have reduced costs further for 2024, however this could have had a detrimental long-term effect for the game,” he said.
“It is essential that we set the game up as best we can for the major revenue events on the horizon in 2025, 2027 and 2029.
“Sales to date for the (2025) Lions tour have been exceptional, both in our market and in the UK. This once-in-12-years event creates the opportunity to repay debt and get over the legacy of Covid-19 that the game is still facing.”

title: New Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt declares preference to select players based in Australia
subtitle: New Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt will rely on one thing in his long-term pursuit of success against the British and Irish Lions in 2025.
content:
To achieve his “massive target” of ensuring Australia is “competitive” against the British and Irish Lions next year, new Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt is set to rely heavily on Super Rugby Pacific players rather than select overseas-based stars.
Despite having a busy 2024 schedule in his maiden year as Wallabies coach, Schmidt is already looking further ahead as he admitted he probably wouldn’t know his best team until December.
However, it’s a line-up seemingly set to be dominated by Australia-based talent rather than those plying their trade at overseas clubs.
“It probably isn’t something we’ve planned,” Schmidt said when asked if he would select any overseas-based stars for the Wallabies’ two Tests against Wales in July.
“We’ve always ben consistent in the messaging around prioritising the players who are playing locally and the reasons for that.
“We do definitely want to select from what is currently available in Australia. I wouldn’t rule it (selecting overseas-based players) out completely but it’s not our priority.”
It’s a selection theme set to continue next year when the Lions tour Australia.
“We want to be as competitive as we can be when the Lions arrive,” Schmidt said.
“That’s my massive target. That’s the pinnacle event. How do we do that? We make sure that we can get as much time with the players, and the players have that time and combinations that they play in at their Super Rugby clubs so that we can build the cohesion that we’re going to need.
“Our priority is the home-based players.”
New Zealander Schmidt is pleased that three of the Wallabies’ six home Tests this year will have afternoon kick-off times, including matches against New Zealand and world champions South Africa.
The Wallabies’ Rugby Championship clash with the Springboks on August 10 at Brisbane’s Suncorp Stadium will start at 2.45pm, while their September 21 Bledisloe Cup battle with the All Blacks at Sydney’s Accor Stadium kicks off at 3.45pm.
“The afternoon kick-offs will create a great atmosphere for players and supporters and we look forward to seeing plenty of gold jerseys in the stands throughout the year,” he said.
“It (also) allows the games to be played in slightly drier conditions, and allows the tempo of the game to be just a little bit quicker.”
While admitting it would be a “little awkward” coaching against New Zealand, Schmidt said he was “motivated” to ensure rugby was as strong as possible in “this corner of the world”.
“That’s a corner we share with the All Blacks, not a corner where we can live in isolation,” he said.
“One of the ways to help each other is try to be as competitive as we can be against each other.
“There’s certainly been a lag on our side of the Tasman, and we’re going to try to roll our sleeves up and close the lag as much as we can.”
July 6: Australia v Wales, Allianz Stadium, Sydney, 7.45pm (AEST)
July 13: Australia v Wales, AAMI Park, Melbourne, 7.45pm (AEST)
July 20: Australia v Georgia, Allianz Stadium, Sydney, 3:45pm (AEST)
August 10: Australia v South Africa, Suncorp Stadium, Brisbane, 2.45pm (AEST)
August 17: Australia v South Africa, Optus Stadium, Perth, 7.45pm (AEST)
September 21: Australia v New Zealand, Accor Stadium, Sydney, 3.45pm (AEST)

title: Damian Browne recalls dramatic 2013 Winterbottom Stakes won by Buffering
subtitle: Group 1 jockey Damian Browne relives Buffering’s victory in an incident-packed Winterbottom Stakes a decade ago where he was hit with a month-long ban and big fine.
content:
Group 1 riding star Damian Browne was so anxious about aeroplane travel that he always sat in aisle seats, but that was the least of the drama as we wind back the clock a decade ago to Buffering’s Group 1 Winterbottom Stakes win.
Nervous traveller Browne, a former Kiwi jockey who had become as Queensland as XXXX beer, had just combined with Buffering for the tough sprinter’s first two Group 1 wins in a golden Melbourne spring.
Incredibly, the 
Group 1 triumphs in the Manikato Stakes and the VRC Sprint Classic led the Buffering team to Perth, where he was sent out the $2 favourite in a race where local hero Barakey ($5.50) was considered the primary threat. 
A cursory look back at the 2013 Winterbottom Stakes result shows Buffering prevailing in a tight result, clinging on to win from charging Peter Moody-trained galloper Moment Of Change. 
But there was much more to the story.
In dramatic post-race scenes, Browne was in trouble with stewards and slapped with a one-month riding suspension and a $5000 fine. 
Browne, sitting outside Barakey and his rider Jason Brown, had seemingly waited an eternity for Brown to either kick-up and hold the lead or let Buffering cross.
The West Australian rider did neither – so Browne took matters into his own hands and crossed, causing interference to Barakey and also to Tony Gollan galloper Spirit Of Boom.
“When it was a tight finish, I was hoping I had won because I had knocked over half the field already,” Browne recalls.
“Jason Brown, who was on the boom Perth horse at the time, just kept being a nuisance.
“I gave him plenty of opportunity to make his mind up.
“He didn’t know what he wanted to do, so I just made his mind up for him.
“I didn’t see Gollan’s thing back on the inside.
“It was a Group 1 race, so yes, you could probably say what I did was worth it.
“But we thought it was a bit harsh getting the fine as well.
“Heathcote paid that fine for me, he reminds me regularly about it.” 
At the time, Browne’s punishment drew outrage with Heathcote saying he should have copped a penalty but the severity was “extraordinary”.
Rival jockey Chris Munce, now a trainer, posted on social media at the time: “What a joke Brownie copping a fine and suspension. The bloke on Barakey should have been rubbed out for stupidity.”
From not being able to win a Group 1, Buffering then kept on winning them for fun and ended his career in 2016 with seven Group 1 wins including winning on the world stage in Dubai. 
Among his Group 1 haul was two Winterbottoms (he went back to win in the west in 2015) and it was his 2013 Winterbottom win, 10 years ago, that Browne says was one of his toughest and showed what Buffering was all about.
“It was a really good win when he went to Perth that year because he was coming to the end of his preparation, and they made him do a bit of work in the race,” Browne said.
“I know he only fell in the last bit, but that just showed his guts and determination.
“It was probably one of his toughest wins.
“We were staying at the casino in Perth, the race was sponsored by the casino at that time.
“They put on a room for us, where all the connections came for the celebrations.
“Buffering used to have a heap of hangers-on – I’ve never seen a horse with so many owners.
“I don’t know how many times somebody told me they had a share in Buffering.” 
 after being rushed to hospital, undergoing emergency surgery for a perforated bowel which was caused by his long-term reliance on anti-inflammatory drugs for a chronic knee injury, which had been surgically repaired 16 times.
He is now much healthier and works as a track supervisor at his local Sunshine Coast track. 
Browne, who recently went with his family to visit Buffering, remembers the Buffering times with great affection but there was also great trepidation at times.
“I hated travel with a passion, I still don’t like it much,” Browne said.
“I used to get bad anxiety in planes, I had to sit in the aisle seats.
“When we were waiting to take off, I would just feel sick all the time, it was a pain.
“Back in the day in New Zealand I had a couple of bad flights on light planes and I think that is where my anxiety with flying stemmed from.
“One day we had to throw out gear out of a light plane because we weren’t going to make it over the trees.
“On another trip, we had to land on a road.”
Ten years on from Buffering’s first Winterbottom triumph, speedy customer

title: Celine Gaudray ‘on fire’ with treble at Caulfield
subtitle: Rising jockey Celine Gaudray drew praise from trainers after continuing her hot streak with a treble at Caulfield.
content:
Rising star Celine Gaudray continued a hot streak in the city with a treble on Saturday at Caulfield.
The 22-year-old’s tally after the treble stood at 10 wins from 30 starts on metropolitan circuits including five inside 24 hours after a double at The Valley last Friday night.
 enjoyed the perfect start to Saturday with her first three rides all winners, including 
Is It Me was Gaudray’s sixth winner in nine starts overall since returning from a short camping trip.
IS IT ME and it's THREE for Celine Gaudray at Caulfield! 
“I’m still a bit unfit,” Gaudray laughed.
“But it was good … it helps with confidence a lot (riding winners).
“If I can keep getting a few winners here and there it is a great help.”
Gaudray, who won the Rising Stars series last season and finished second in the apprentice premiership behind Carleen Hefel, rode a personal best midweek city four-timer last April.
Is It Me won comfortably at the finish but Gaudray had some doubt in the run.
“I didn’t expect to be that far back but he was actually off the bridle a long way out and I just kept niggling just to stay in contact,” Gaudray said.
“I actually didn’t think he was doing too much but as soon as we straightened up he was really good through the line. 
“He’s extremely competitive and when he hit the front he stopped and waited for a few to catch up, he was strong.” 
Trainer Daniel Bowman praised Gaudray’s ride on talented gelding Is It Me, a $2.60 favourite in the 1200m Benchmark 70.
“That was perfect, (she) kept him in plenty of galloping room, let him track up behind one of the other chances (runner-up Pink Beau Ty),” Bowman said.
Earlier, trainer John Leek Jr, who saddled Regal Power, led the Gaudray appreciation.
“Celine is on fire, she rode the horse perfect,” Leek Jr said.
“Sometimes it’s very hard to get the horse in the right position, she looked like she was going to get into a bit of trouble at one stage, I was a bit concerned, but anyway, her skill is very, very good.”
Female jockeys dominated the card on Saturday, winning six of the 10 winners.
Apprentice jockey Tatum Bull scored a race-to-race double on Ginger ‘N’ Pink and My Boy Birmingham while champion rider Jamie Kah opened the card aboard Traffic Warden.
Regal Power moved closer to the $5 million prizemoney mark with a long-awaited and well-deserved 10th win from 40 starts.
The Bob Peters-owned multiple Group 1 and All-Star Mile winner was two years between wins but good placement and a classy ride from rising star Celine Gaudray sealed the deal.
“He’s very deserving of today’s win,” Gaudray said.

 enjoyed the perfect start to Saturday with her first three rides all winners, including

title: William Pike backing Bob Peters to return as a dominant force in WA
subtitle: Ahead of his bid to win a sixth Group 1 Railway Stakes, William Pike opens up on the racing dynamic in Perth where big-time owner Bob Peters is no longer dominating like he once was.
content:
For many years, William Pike and Bob Peters went together like fish and chips, bread and butter and shoes and socks.
Almost every time you looked at a Perth race, wizard of the west jockey 
But Peters doesn’t have the dominant presence winning races he once did.
He famously split with trainers 
Pike has kept on riding winners – he is the length of the straight ahead in the Perth jockeys’ premiership this season after choosing to base himself at home again after some time testing the waters in Sydney.
But, as Pike prepares to try to win his sixth Group 1 Railway Stakes and his fifth in sixth years, he quickly dismisses any suggestions that it’s been good for him getting outside the Peters’ bubble when riding winners.
“
“
“The support I am getting from everyone in Perth has still been really great.
“The difference with Bob Peters not firing as strongly as he was for all those years, is I don’t know where my next good horse is going to be. 
“Finding the next horse to win a big race is really hard right now.” 
Pike will be attempting to win his sixth Group 1 Railway Stakes – and his fifth in six years – when he is legged aboard Grant and Alana Williams-trained equal favourite ($4.60) 
All of Pike’s five Railway wins have come for Team Williams – but there is now a stark difference after Peters split with them and they had a stable rebuild.
• 
“Bob Peters will kick back,” Pike insisted.
“I don't think there’s an entire changing of the guard, but as with all things, it just takes a few years for the process to play out.
“When he did a changeover of trainers, quite a few of his good horses went east and a few other things happened.”
Pike still believes he is in pole position to claim the Railway again.
Alsephina may not have won this preparation, but the five-year-old mare has finished runner-up twice and both runs have impressed Pike.
Importantly, Pike says, Grant and Alana Williams know how to peak their horses for the Railway and Alsephina gets in with a lovely weight (53kg).
In the last nine years, the Railway has not been won by any horse who has carried more than 53.5kg.
• 
“I think Alsephina is the real deal, and you know because she is trained by Grant and Alana who know how to win this race, she will be peaking on the day,” Pike said.
“There was a deliberate plan to make sure she got to this race on the minimum (weight).
“There has been a pretty strong formula that low weights generally go best in the race. 
“She has picked her way through the grades really well and she was carrying the flag for the stable while they were rebuilding. 
“With WA racing you don't know if you are a good horse until you go in these sort races, we don't get to spar against the big boys (from the eastern seaboard) too often.” 
With a heatwave striking Perth this week, Pike has downplayed the scorching temperatures being a potential ace up the sleeve of the local Perth horses.
He hopes the Ascot track plays fairly on Saturday.
“The track is going to be interesting,” Pike said.
“I'm normally not a jockey to complain about (track) patterns too often, but there has definitely been patterns in the track this year.
“You’ve either needed to be in the first four in the run to win – or you can’t be in the first four and win.
“It’s often played to one extreme or the other.”
Pike also has a sparkling hope in the Group 2 WA Guineas (1600m) where he rides $2.90 equal favourite 
“She is only a little filly, but she has a great can-do attitude,” Pike said.
“The whole way along, she had a stablemate that we thought was better (Written Melody).
“But the stablemate has gone to the paddock and this filly is still here punching away.”
The Railway Stakes card has been pushed back due to the heatwave, with 39 degree temperatures now forecast on Saturday.

content:

Rarely is champion Queensland 
Gollan always knew he had a serious horse on his hands – that was on show when Antino finished a narrow runner-up behind Attrition in the Group 1 Toorak Handicap at Caulfield last spring.
There had been some alarm bells ringing about Antino’s winter carnival prospects after some underwhelming recent jumpouts.
ANTINO'S BACK WITH A BANG! ðª 
And Gollan had to abort a Group 1 Doncaster Mile campaign in the autumn when Antino had some minor niggles and Gollan wasn’t 100 per cent happy with him.
All that was a distant memory as Antino flashed home to score the Victory and zoomed into become $6 equal favourite with Magic Time for next month’s Stradbroke Handicap.
Pulling the pin on five-year-old Antino’s Sydney autumn campaign now looks a masterstroke.
“It means a lot this win, I love this horse,” Gollan said.
“This is a good horse and he just does things that other horses can’t.
“He is a different animal.
“At home you wouldn’t know he is any good, he just pops along and does what he does.
“But he is a really good galloper. 
“We had to pull back on him for the autumn because I just wasn’t happy with him, and really target the winter, it meant a lot to run well today because the Stradbroke is our grand final.
“He is a proper racehorse, he really is.”
Antino was at one point the favourite for last year’s Stradbroke but didn’t make the final field.
Gollan has no such worries this year and can sit back and smoke his pipe and plot the best way to Stradbroke glory, most likely deploying Antino next in the 
The Victory triumph was another feather in the cap of jockey 
“I said to Vlad, this horse can sustain a run longer than any horse I’ve ever trained,” Gollan said.
“He certainly had to do that today. 
“Not only was he slow away, he was off the bridle mid-race and he never travelled at all. 
“He makes really hard work of it, but I knew once they got inside the final furlong they were never going to beat him. 
“When he pins his ears back and he has a go, he’s a different beast.”
Antino was well-backed into $4.40, beating home runner-up 
Drifting favourite

title: Ashford Street makes winning debut at Caulfield for new trainer Tom Dabernig
subtitle: Tom Dabernig’s exceptional month continued at Caulfield with Ashford Street winning in his stable debut.
content:
Caulfield winner Ashford Street might have joined the Tom Dabernig stable at the perfect time.
Former trainer Ken Elford was getting on in years so decided to send the talented sprinter to the 
Will proudly led in 
Ashford Street ($10) raced a touch wide under apprentice 
ASHFORD STREET NAILS IT ON THE LINE! ðª 
“The horse came to me in great order,” Dabernig said.
“It’s a real sense of timing because we got the horse in great shape and brought him along.
“We didn’t quite have him ready at Warrnambool and we were half trying to have him right for the Wangoom but he’s probably more of a 1000m horse than a 12(00m horse).
“We thought this race looked ideal with the claim of Jayla Kennedy.”
Ashford Street continued a brilliant month for the Dabernig camp, becoming the Warrnambool’s stable’s 12th winner from its last 50 runners.
Dabernig had three winners on his adopted home track during the three-day carnival midweek.
The former Lindsay Park trainer said his stable was now fully operational after being hindered by insufficient stabling until about eight weeks ago.
“We were a bit restricted at the start with the stabling numbers but now we’ve got stabling for 60,” Dabernig said.
“We’ve only had the extra 20 for about two months so we’ve got the stables full.”
Daberning said the shift to Warrnambool and the facilities available in the area prompted him to evaluate and adjust his training style, which was now bearing fruit.
He said the availability of nearby beaches was a great help to his team, offsetting issues such as staff and travelling distances to the city tracks.
“I think any place takes a bit of time to work it out and I’ve had to adjust the way I train them a little bit to the Lindsay Park days to try and work out what works and what doesn’t,” Dabernig said.
“The beach is a big asset and that’s something I’ve really embraced.
“I went to Warrnambool to utilise the beach and even though there’s extra work and labour and cost in doing it, I really think the benefits outweigh things like the travel times, the horses seem to recover much better over the next few days when you get them home.”
Dabernig said Ashford Street would compete in similar races to Saturday’s Caulfield assignment through the winter months before a possible shot at the Group 3 Sir John Monash Stakes in July.
Timing was everything as 
 had made a big impression with wins at Pakenham at his first two starts and the $2.60 favourite looked set to stay undefeated halfway down the straight.
However, favourite backers’ confidence quickly eroded as jockey Daniel Moor brought The Shaper ($12) with the perfectly timed run in the last 150m to grab Angland on the line.
The Shaper won at Sandown two runs back before a narrow defeat at Cranbourne at his previous outing.
Co-trainer Sam Freedman said taking The Shaper back to last was the right way to ride the son of Street boss, who posted his second win in five starts at Caulfield.
.
“Last time out at Cranbourne, he landed outside the lead and that certainly the way we needed him ridden but in a small field, it ended up like that,” Freedman, who trains The Shaper in partnership with his father Anthony, said.
“He’s much better when he can just balance up.
“I think the slight query on the favourite might have been the trip and we were quite happy to let it all unfold and be the last ones to have a crack.
“Daniel gave him a great steer today.”

“The horse came to me in great order,” Dabernig said.
“It’s a real sense of timing because we got the horse in great shape and brought him along.
“We didn’t quite have him ready at Warrnambool and we were half trying to have him right for the Wangoom but he’s probably more of a 1000m horse than a 12(00m horse).
“We thought this race looked ideal with the claim of Jayla Kennedy.”
Ashford Street continued a brilliant month for the Dabernig camp, becoming the Warrnambool’s stable’s 12th winner from its last 50 runners.
Dabernig had three winners on his adopted home track during the three-day carnival midweek.
The former Lindsay Park trainer said his stable was now fully operational after being hindered by insufficient stabling until about eight weeks ago.
“We were a bit restricted at the start with the stabling numbers but now we’ve got stabling for 60,” Dabernig said.
“We’ve only had the extra 20 for about two months so we’ve got the stables full.”
Daberning said the shift to Warrnambool and the facilities available in the area prompted him to evaluate and adjust his training style, which was now bearing fruit.
He said the availability of nearby beaches was a great help to his team, offsetting issues such as staff and travelling distances to the city tracks.
“I think any place takes a bit of time to work it out and I’ve had to adjust the way I train them a little bit to the Lindsay Park days to try and work out what works and what doesn’t,” Dabernig said.
“The beach is a big asset and that’s something I’ve really embraced.
“I went to Warrnambool to utilise the beach and even though there’s extra work and labour and cost in doing it, I really think the benefits outweigh things like the travel times, the horses seem to recover much better over the next few days when you get them home.”

title: Hours spent watching horse racing on TV can help deliver Kyle Wilson-Taylor The Quokka upset with Kiwi raider Waitak
subtitle: Group 1-winning jockey Kyle Wilson-Taylor is a self-confessed racing “nerd” who is aiming to ride a Kiwi galloper to glory in the $5m The Quokka in Perth on Saturday.
content:
Self-confessed “racing nerd” Kyle Wilson-Taylor is on the hunt for the 
, who broke through at Group 1 level when winning last year's Tatt’s Tiara on Palaisipan, is preparing to ride Kiwi invader 
Queenslander Wilson-Taylor has never ridden in Perth before – he has only been to Western Australia once on a holiday with his fiancee and fellow Brisbane rider Angela Jones.
But, as usual, he will leave no stone unturned in a fastidious preparation for the richest race he has ever ridden in.
“I'm a bit of a nerd when it comes to racing and I love watching racing and I watch races wherever they are,” Wilson-Taylor said.
“I do it to improve myself and also because I am very passionate about the sport.
“I want to be a world-class rider and I think you have got to have that level of obsession to continue to improve. 
“When I get home on a Saturday from riding in Brisbane, the Perth races are still going and I keep a good eye on them.”
Wilson-Taylor has never ridden in a $5m race before and got the chance due to a foundation set during last year’s Queensland winter carnival.
The young hoop established a working relationship with ace New Zealand trainers 
Scott and O’Sullivan have called up Wilson-Taylor again for the mission on Waitak.
Two starts ago, Waitak stormed home from last to score an astonishing win in the Group 1 Railway Stakes in New Zealand.
He needs to step up to another level on Saturday, taking on some of Australia’s best sprinters in The Quokka.
Wilson-Taylor feels he will need to pick his way through the field, similar to how champion jockey Damien Oliver did when famously winning his farewell ride on Munhamek in the $1.5m Gold Rush in Perth last December.

“It would be nice to get a chunk of that $5 million.”

title: Stable Of Stars founder Grant Williams reveals near-death experience ahead of King Colorado’s Australian Guineas tilt
subtitle: King Colorado has taken his large group of “owners” on an amazing ride, but it wouldn’t have happened had Stable Of Stars founder Grant Williams not survived a major stroke.
content:
A huge group of racing lovers have been on the ride of their lives with Group 1 star King Colorado, but their incredible journey would not have taken off if Grant Williams hadn’t come back from the dead.
Williams, the founder of the Stable Of Stars which leases shares in 
But only weeks before, Williams was watching a State of Origin rugby league match on television at his NSW central coast home when he suffered a life-threatening stroke.
It was only quick thinking by his sister who wasted no time calling an ambulance, and the proximity of a nearby hospital with a dedicated stroke ward, which saved Williams’ life.
“I was watching State of Origin and I didn’t even know I was having a stroke, it was only because my sister said that I was talking gobbledygook that she called an ambulance,” Williams said.
“It only took the paramedics two or three minutes to get to me, I was cursing my sister saying ‘you’ve ruined the State of Origin for me’.
“The paramedics walked in the door and spent 30 seconds with me and they said ‘you’re having a stroke, let’s go’.
“They told me I had less than 30 minutes otherwise I’d be dead.
“I was lucky that Gosford Hospital has a dedicated stroke unit, I got to hospital quickly and they did thrombolysis on me, so that blasted the blood clot.
“They said the blood clot in my brain was so big that in 30 minutes I would have been dead.
“It took me a couple of days to get my speech back, but the only deficiency I’ve got from now is some is some short-term memory loss that nobody would really notice.”
The launch of Stable Of Stars was delayed by 12 months due to Williams’ major health battle but 
King Colorado provided one of 2023’s most extraordinary racing stories, partly “owned” by a group of 48 owners and with as much as $151 bet leading into the JJ Atkins and then officially he was backed from $41 to $14 to score an incredible win. 
The eclectic Aussie group who leases the horse from his breeder Sheikh Mohammed bin Khalifa Al Maktoum includes
King Colorado had a disappointing spring campaign but has since returned with a bang in two runner-up finishes this year.
He now lines up as one of the leading fancies in the 
The high interest from farms for a potential stud deal, which diminished in spring when the colt didn’t win a race during the carnival, will return if the Ciaron Maher-trained galloper can soar to glory in the Guineas. 
For Williams, 62, he is simply glad he is still around to see the moment.
“I know it is a bit of a cliche how people say when they have a near-death experience, their life changes, but it really does,” Williams said.
“I get an extra great buzz out of life now and I know all my ‘owners’ in King Colorado are having a really great time.
“After he won the JJ Atkins, as a two-year-old Group 1 winner, everyone was saying he was going to be a sought after stallion.
“There were a number of (stud) farms that were interested in him, but when he came back in spring that interest waned because we didn’t win a race during spring.
“If he wins the Guineas, I am sure that interest (from stud farms) will be back.”

title: Smart mare The Map on Melbourne Cup path after impressive win at Morphettville
subtitle: Improving stayer The Map returned with a dominant win at Morphettville and will now chase a golden ticket into the Melbourne Cup.
content:
Connections of 
The smart staying mare – trained by 
“I just love that horse (The Map), every time she does something like that my heart explodes, I just love her,” MacGillivray said.
All things permitting the mare will now head to the Listed Andrew Ramsden Stakes (2800m) at Flemington on May 18, which offers a golden ticket to the Melbourne Cup for the winner. 
“The thing about the Melbourne Cup is that especially now, it’s harder for a local horse to get in it,” she said. 
“That’s the start. We’re nearly in it, but we keep giving ourselves that chance.”
THIS IS GIRL POWER, IT'S 
Kah was also thrilled to win another race for the Clarken and MacGillivray stable.
“Every time I ride The Map for these guys, it feels like I win a Group 1. It’s awesome, it’s a great feeling,” an elated Kah said. 
Trevor Day and Jeffrey Maund combined to win the opener on the card with tough stayer 
“To be honest I thought her trial the other day was impressive, first time tongue tie, the vet recommended that, so we tried that with her and she’s been working the house down,” Boyce said. 
Another Murray Bridge trainer saluted in race three, with Classy Kenny producing an impressive win for John Hickmott an Carrina Riggs. 
Melbourne Cup-winning hoop Blake Shinn steered him up the inside of the field on the straight to successfully run down tearaway leader Sunzou. 
“He’s (Classy Kenny) been working a treat, more thanks to Carrina than me, she’s been holding the fort the last few weeks and she’s done a great job,” Hickmott said.
After nailing an upset win in race two, Pannell was ready to blow away punters again, steering longshot East Indiaman to victory for Darren McLeod at odds of $34.
Sir Kingsford strode to the front and set up a strong tempo under Kayla Crowther in the Provincial Pathways Final (1800m).
The smart gelding now has six wins from 16-career starts for the Searle and Callanan stable – who had their heart in their mouths as a result of his run and gun style out in front.
“I don’t think my heart has beaten so fast for so long,” Nichole Searle said, who trains in partnership with husband Gary and daughter Brianna. 
“It was a bit nerve wrecking the last 100m, but he just toughs it out, if they get to him – he just lifts again.”
The gelding carried a massive 61kg to victory in Saturday’s Provincial Pathways Final (1800m). 
“I was huffing and puffing getting the saddle back to the horse, Kayla (Crowther) is only tiny, there was a lot of dead weight so it was a huge effort from him today – he just lifted and lifted.”
Hayes’ filly Poifect was a dominant winner in the Listed Adelaide Guineas (1600m), crossing from barrier 12 under Michael Dee to take up the lead, and kick clear at the top of the straight. 
Pannell showed why he’s still one of the state’s best riders on the nine-race Derby card, finishing with a treble after winning the last race aboard Delightful Shecky for Dylan Caboche. 
Kah snared a double on the day with The Map and Coco Sun in the Group 1 SA Derby.

title: Ceejay Graham scores emotional feature victory in Group 2 Queensland Guineas
subtitle: Leading apprentice Ceejay Graham was fighting back tears after claiming the biggest win of her career in the Group 2 Queensland Guineas at Eagle Farm.
content:
Ceejay Graham went through hell and back with a series of injuries which saw her on the sidelines for an extended period, but the leading apprentice was on cloud nine on Saturday after an emotional win aboard 
The popular rider used to drive six hours to the races in Brisbane and suffered a broken back along with fractured wrists, but they were all a distant memory after 
Punters honed in on other runners, but Graham was able to withhold the might of Godolphin in a two-horse battle against Razors to earn the praise of Portelli, who will head to the Group 3 Rough Habit Plate in a fortnight with the brother to Golden Slipper winner Fireburn. 
KINTYRE closes out the Eagle Farm card in style! ð 
“It feels incredible, I don’t have the words to describe it really,” Graham said while holding back tears.
“I didn’t think I would get these opportunities with the time I’ve had off, but to be back here and winning that race makes every bit of hard work worthwhile.
“I couldn’t be more grateful to Gary and the owners. Gary has been such a big supporter of female jockeys for many years, and hopefully this will put me in good stead as I come out of my apprenticeship.”
As a short-priced favourite to win the coveted Brisbane apprentice title, Graham produced a copybook ride aboard the Sydney raider. 
“The race couldn’t have worked out any better,” he said.
“From the good alley, we got such a sweet run and were able to make the leaders do enough work to bring us into the race. 
“When the leader peeled out I knew we were going to have such a sweet travel through. I couldn’t believe it when he poked his head in front, it’s a feeling like no other.”
Portelli has long been an admirer of Graham’s work and said it was a long-term plan to repay her. 
“I’ve been watching Ceejay since I came up here, she rode a winner for me on Spaceboy and helped me out when we had Fireburn up here, so I wanted to repay her for helping me out,” he said. 
“I put her on this horse in a Group 2, I told her not to be worried about going up the inside because it’s not inferior ground. He’s a tough horse and she rode him a treat.”
Portelli said he is unlikely to press on to the Group 1 Queensland Derby following the Rough Habit Plate later this month, with the super rich Golden Eagle proving to be an attractive lure in the spring.

title: Jamie Kah claims first South Australian Group 1 success with Coco Sun in SA Derby at Morphettville
subtitle: Hometown hero Jamie Kah finally landed her first Group 1 in South Australia after riding Coco Sun to victory in the Group 1 SA Derby on Saturday.
content:
Star South Australian jockey Jamie Kah has added a hometown Group 1 to her remarkable list of accomplishments in the saddle, steering 
 made the ride look effortless, steering the filly to the rail early in the $1 million feature before working into a gap that opened up at the top of the straight. 
The 
“It’s all I wanted,” Kah, now a 13-time Group 1 winner, said.
“It’s just amazing, the club has put up such good races this year, it was never going to be easy.
“I had a great ride today, I had a great ride last weekend but it obviously didn’t go my way – but today it did.
“For the old boss too (Tony McEvoy), he’s put up with me for a long time too so he deserves it.”
COCO SUN WINS THE SOUTH AUSTRALIAN DERBY! âï¸
Kah didn’t miss her first boss either, Strathalbyn trainer John Macmillan. 
“John (Macmillan) is here, so I’ve got to thank Johnny. He set me up, got me going and had me stay with Mick Price and got me going there and then I got going with Tony,“ she said.
“I had so many years here riding with Tony and so many winners and he looked after me so well, so it’s nice to repay him.
“He put up with a lot back in the day too.
“All that I wanted to do was ride a Group 1 winner in Adelaide in front of Mum and Dad and family and all those that have supported me.”
A delighted Tony McEvoy was full of praise for Kah post-race. 
“Jamie had so much faith in her. She said to me she wanted to bounce out and put her there, and the only question I had was the 2500(m), but you don’t argue with Jamie Kah,” McEvoy said. 
“I can’t thank her enough for what she did for my brand and my stable. She kept beating me and I thought ‘how am I going to change this?’ The only way I could do it was to get her on board. 
“Sadly she outgrew me, which was always going to be the way, but she’s been a star forever and I love her.” 
Coco Sun now looks set to tackle the looming Queensland winter carnival.
“It’s five weeks now to the Queensland Oaks. In five weeks time Terry Jarvis (owner) will be looking for some sun out of New Zealand, so if she’s well, we’ll go to the Oaks,” he said.
It was Kah’s second feature win of the day, after she claimed the Group 3 Queen Elizabeth Cup (2500m) aboard The Map for Dan Clarken and Oopy MacGillivray.

title: Peter and Paul Snowden’s import Coco Jamboo impresses in Hawkesbury Crown in Australian debut
subtitle: Imported mare Coco Jamboo was in fine tune when she scored a game win in the Group 3 Hawkesbury Crown at her Australian debut.
content:
Coco Jamboo, named after a hit song and a direct descendant of the legendary Northern Dancer, made an auspicious Australian debut at the Hawkesbury stand-alone meeting on Saturday.
Trainers 
“It’s not easy to win with these imports at their first Australian starts,” Peter Snowden said.
“You are going in cold, you don’t know much about them, and you want to see them run a few times to learn about them as our racing is different altogether to what they are used to.
“But occasionally you get these imported horses who take to our racing and training straight away like Huetor. The good ones can do it so for Coco Jamboo to win a stakes race first-up is a great result.”
A fantastic finish to the G3 Hawkesbury Crown as Coco Jamboo ticks off her first win in Australia! ð
Coco Jamboo ($41), well ridden by 
The Snowden stable had four of the top seven finishers in the Crown with 
Former English mare Coco Jamboo arrived in Sydney with a record of three wins from 14 starts and her Hawkesbury win was her first stakes success.
But Snowden recalled his initial impression of Coco Jamboo was hardly enthusiastic.
“When I saw the video of her in England, she looked a nice mare,” Snowden said.
“But I must say when she arrived at the stables I thought ‘you looked much bigger on TV’.
“Then we started to work her along a bit and she really started to flourish.
“Tommy Sherry rode her early in her preparation and wanted to stick with her. He noticed something from day one. She’s a nice mare.”
Coco Jamboo, named after a 1996 hit song from the German group Mr President, gave Snowden a seventh Hawkesbury Crown after previous wins with Nancy (2016), Aerobatics (2013-14), Kanzan (2011), Serenissima (2010) and Sung (2008).
Bloodstock agent Will Johnson sources many of the Snowden stable’s talented imports and he has seemingly struck again with Coco Jamboo.
“We thought she had a really good racing profile for fast ground as she can react off a quick tempo which we have here,” Johnson said.
“I lived and worked in Newmarket (England) for a while and got to know (trainer) Marco Botti really well and he recommended this mare for Australia.
“A good friend of mine in England who does a lot of form also highly recommended her and stayed in for 25 per cent of the mare.
“She cost 160,000 guineas which is roughly about $A350,000 but she is certainly worth that now.”
Coco Jamboo’s Group 3 win sends her value as a potential broodmare into the stratosphere as she has the Northern Dancer bloodlines coursing through her veins.
Northern Dancer was a champion racehorse who won 14 of his 18 starts including the 1964 Kentucky Derby before achieving even greater fame at stud, becoming one of the greatest and most influential stallions of all-time.
The legendary thoroughbred is the sire of champions like Nijinsky, El Gran Senor, Fanfreluche, Sadler’s Wells, The Minstrel and Storm Bird.
But Coco Jamboo’s immediate future is on the racetrack with Snowden considering taking the mare to the Group 3 $250,000 Dark Jewel Classic (1400m) at Scone in two weeks.
“I’ll think about the Dark Jewel,” Snowden said.
“She is used to racing every three or four weeks in England so I will see how she pulls up first.
“We could even take her straight to Brisbane and get her ready for the Dane Ripper Stakes and Tatts Tiara.”
Snowden said Ghaanati and Mirra View are two mares his stable will almost certainly send to Scone for the Dark Jewel Classic.
“Ghaanati didn’t have a lot of luck today, she has run a very good race,” Snowden said. 
“Mirra View is also likely to go to Scone but we need rain for her.”
Godolphin’s superbly-bred sprinter Parisal enhanced her reputation as a first-up specialist with a brilliant return to racing at Hawkesbury on Saturday.
 showed her class with an emphatic win in the Listed $200,000 Hawkesbury XXXX Gold Rush (1100m).
Hall of Famer Darren Beadman, representing trainer 
“Parisal’s two (barrier) trials have been fantastic, her first-up record is very good and 1100m is her pet distance,” Beadman said.
“It was a lovely ride by 
Parisal wins first up in the Listed 
Parisal was confidently backed into $2.80 favouritism and had punters cheering as she seized control of the race in the straight and defeated 
“I had a barrier which enabled me to just sneak into the race on Parisal,” Lloyd said.
“When she joined the leaders in the straight she really wanted to win the race.”
The Gold Rush was Parisal’s third stakes win and the fifth victory of her 13-start career, taking her prizemoney to over $700,000.
She is particularly lethal fresh with three wins and a second placing from her only four first-up attempts.
Parisal ran the Hawkesbury 1100m in 1m 2.32s including a stunning final 600m sectional of 32.72.
Beadman said Parisal is likely to go to Scone next where either the Ortensia Stakes (1100m) or the Luskin Star Stakes (1300m) are possible targets before joining Godolphin’s Brisbane winter carnival team.
Beadman said there was merit in the run of minor placegetter, Spacewalk.
“There is not a great deal between Parisal and Spacewalk,” Beadman said.
“But Parisal had the right run and handled the occasion a lot better today.
Parisal is by Astern out of Circular, which makes the mare a half-sister to Godolphin’s Newmarket Handicap winner, Cylinder.
The speedy mare will be a valuable addition to Godolphin-Darley’s broodmare band when she does finally retire from racing.
Parisal is a product of one of the racing and breeding giant’s most famous and enduring families as her fifth grand-dam is the celebrated broodmare Shadea, mother of the champion racehorse and sire, Lonhro.

Northern Dancer was a champion racehorse who won 14 of his 18 starts including the 1964 Kentucky Derby before achieving even greater fame at stud, becoming one of the greatest and most influential stallions of all-time.
The legendary thoroughbred is the sire of champions like Nijinsky, El Gran Senor, Fanfreluche, Sadler’s Wells, The Minstrel and Storm Bird.
But Coco Jamboo’s immediate future is on the racetrack with Snowden considering taking the mare to the Group 3 $250,000 Dark Jewel Classic (1400m) at Scone in two weeks.
“I’ll think about the Dark Jewel,” Snowden said.
“She is used to racing every three or four weeks in England so I will see how she pulls up first.
“We could even take her straight to Brisbane and get her ready for the Dane Ripper Stakes and Tatts Tiara.”
Snowden said Ghaanati and Mirra View are two mares his stable will almost certainly send to Scone for the Dark Jewel Classic.
“Ghaanati didn’t have a lot of luck today, she has run a very good race,” Snowden said. 
“Mirra View is also likely to go to Scone but we need rain for her.”
Godolphin’s superbly-bred sprinter Parisal enhanced her reputation as a first-up specialist with a brilliant return to racing at Hawkesbury on Saturday.
 showed her class with an emphatic win in the Listed $200,000 Hawkesbury XXXX Gold Rush (1100m).
Hall of Famer Darren Beadman, representing trainer 
“Parisal’s two (barrier) trials have been fantastic, her first-up record is very good and 1100m is her pet distance,” Beadman said.
“It was a lovely ride by 
Parisal wins first up in the Listed 
Parisal was confidently backed into $2.80 favouritism and had punters cheering as she seized control of the race in the straight and defeated 
“I had a barrier which enabled me to just sneak into the race on Parisal,” Lloyd said.
“When she joined the leaders in the straight she really wanted to win the race.”
The Gold Rush was Parisal’s third stakes win and the fifth victory of her 13-start career, taking her prizemoney to over $700,000.
She is particularly lethal fresh with three wins and a second placing from her only four first-up attempts.
Parisal ran the Hawkesbury 1100m in 1m 2.32s including a stunning final 600m sectional of 32.72.
Beadman said Parisal is likely to go to Scone next where either the Ortensia Stakes (1100m) or the Luskin Star Stakes (1300m) are possible targets before joining Godolphin’s Brisbane winter carnival team.
Beadman said there was merit in the run of minor placegetter, Spacewalk.
“There is not a great deal between Parisal and Spacewalk,” Beadman said.
“But Parisal had the right run and handled the occasion a lot better today.
Parisal is by Astern out of Circular, which makes the mare a half-sister to Godolphin’s Newmarket Handicap winner, Cylinder.
The speedy mare will be a valuable addition to Godolphin-Darley’s broodmare band when she does finally retire from racing.
Parisal is a product of one of the racing and breeding giant’s most famous and enduring families as her fifth grand-dam is the celebrated broodmare Shadea, mother of the champion racehorse and sire, Lonhro.

 blitzed his rivals on debut at Cranbourne at his only run last time in. He has the class to score first-up on Friday.

 raced on the speed and tried hard at Cranbourne last week. He’ll be hard to run down despite the seven-day back-up.

 was too good when leading throughout at Geelong and could figure in the finish again despite a tricky draw.

 is on the fresh side after scoring last time out. He can bob up again in an even contest at Cranbourne.

title: Nikita Tszyu has hit back at his brother’s ‘ignorant’ critics saying there is ‘no use listening to idiots’
subtitle: Nikita Tszyu has opted to use the same corner staff for his first title defence, despite the team being under fire for their treatment in brother Tim’s bloodbath fight just weeks ago.
content:
Nikita Tszyu wants an ‘arousing’ and bloody Australian super-welterweight title defence against Danilo Creati on April 24, and 
when he makes the first defence of his Australian title at the Hordern Pavilion.
He also challenged the elusive Creati to a firefight, and called for longtime Tszyu rival Michael Zerafa to retire from the sport.
Nikita was ringside for 
“It’s just all ignorance, they don’t know what’s going on, so I tend not to look at what other people say,” Tszyu told this masthead. “I consider a lot of people in this sport idiots, so there’s no use in listening to idiots talk.
“Even some of the apparent professionals saying they couldn’t stop the cut.
“Our team doctor, Dr Bill, said if it’s a cut through the vein like it was, there’s no way you could stop it in a minute. You need 15 minute’s worth of pressure to stop the bleeding.
“It’s like putting a bandaid on a hose and expecting it to hold. It’s impossible and they did everything they could.
“The corner did their best.
“They’ll be in my corner. Nothing changes, we’re family.”
Nikita is adamant Tim won the fight, and was left in awe at what his older brother pulled off.
“I was shocked with how much blood he lost,” he said. “I get dizzy after taking a little sample of blood for the doctor and Tim lost a litre of it and was still able to perform.
“It’s insane. That heart, it’s not something you can train, it’s something you’re born with.
“The fact he couldn’t see and was still dominating the fight was amazing. The hurdles he had to overcome, and he’s fighting blind…I’m very proud to have him as a brother.”
Having seen what Tim did, Nikita wants his own fight with Creati to be as bloody as possible.
“Seeing all the blood it was quite arousing for me,” he said of Tim’s fight. “I’m attracted to that kind of gruesomeness and if we can get it happening in this fight I’m happy for it.
“I’m happy to be cut.
“I’d love there to be messiness, I’d love to stain the ring, my boxing shorts, his boxing shorts.”
Former five-time Italian national champion Creati is an elusive and awkward test for Tszyu in his eighth professional fight.
The 8-1-1 underdog has an upset win over Cameron Hammond, took Michael Zerafa the distance and is only too happy to oblige Tszyu’s preference for putting on a spectacle. 
“I love it,” he said. “I’m keen to go for a fight like that. I never step back.
“He’s a human being like everyone, with flaws. We saw these flaws with Dylan Biggs and with Jack Brubaker.
“He’s fragile. His chin is fragile, and we’re gonna go for it.”
If Tszyu can get past Creati, he has a mouth-watering hit list of domestic opponents lined up, including Brock Jarvis and Koen Mazoudier.
“We sparred a couple of times in the amateurs,” Nikita said of Jarvis. “It was just when he was starting off as well.
“I remember kicking his ass. So, let’s go again, we’ll see how much he’s improved. With small 10 ounce gloves (in the pros) and over 10 rounds…Poor Brocky.”
Zerafa is another potential future opponent for Tszyu, following the Melbournian’s second round knockout defeat to Erislandy Lara on Tim’s undercard.
The rivalry between Zerafa and Team Tszyu goes back years, but Nikita scoffs at suggestions he should fight Zerafa.
“It’s amusing to me,” laughed. “I’ll fight him, I’ll fight anyone.
“But at this point, I don’t think he needs another fight like that on his resume. He doesn’t need another loss.
“He’s achieved a lot already, 
“After the loss, that beautiful knockout to Lara, I don’t know what he wants to do.
“It’s a hard one to come back from.”

title: ‘She said yes’: Boxing champ Ryan Garcia announces engagement to Aussie adult film star
subtitle: Boxing superstar Ryan Garcia has announced his engagement to Australian adult film star Savannah Bond in a heartfelt video.
content:
Boxing superstar Ryan Garcia has announced his engagement to Australian adult film star Savannah Bond.
The news comes just days before Garcia’s super-lightweight title clash with Devin Haney this Sunday (AEST).
Garcia, 25, took to social media to share a video of him proposing to Savannah.
In the video, which you can watch below, Garcia can be seen down on one knee asking for the 33-year-old Australian’s hand in marriage, with the video ending with the couple kissing.
Taking to social media, a jubilant Garcia wrote: “She said yes!!!!!!. I’m so happy and motivated going into my fight now.
“Let’s gooooooo. Lets go for real. She’s my wife or future wifey but still very very happy.
“Everyone have a great day.”
Savannah, who has starred in more than 100 adult films, has shared posts alongside Garcia on the her Instagram page.
Garcia is father to three children, two daughters and a son.
He drew criticism when he announced his divorce to ex-wife Andrea Celina just hours after the birth of their son in January of this year.
Andrea is also the mother to one of the American’s daughters.
Earlier this year 
Garcia has also hit headlines recently for his alarming social media activity.
Last month he shared an alarming video on his pages which suggesting he died after having his “throat slit”.
While he shared a follow-up video saying he was okay, along with ex-wife Andrea sharing a worried post online, there was more trouble as he started sharing conspiracy theories online.
He shared a theory about the Bohemian Grove, a private community north of San Francisco and west of Santa Rosa, and reposted a video claiming he was held captive there.
His activity online has also seen him appear to claim there will be an earthquake on June 6th.
Garcia has also made calls to “free” controversial influencer Andrew Tate after he was arrested and released in Romania with a sexual assault warrant in the UK.
In terms of his upcoming bout, Garcia and Haney have already clashed six times as amateur fighters with their outcomes ending 3-3.
This will be their first as pro’s but their seventh overall, with Haney’s WBC super-lightweight on the line.
The fight will take place on April 21 (AEST) at the Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York.

en_title: ‘She said yes’: Boxing champ Ryan Garcia announces engagement to Aussie adult film star
en_content:
Boxing superstar Ryan Garcia has announced his engagement to Australian adult film star Savannah Bond.
The news comes just days before Garcia’s super-lightweight title clash with Devin Haney this Sunday (AEST).
Garcia, 25, took to social media to share a video of him proposing to Savannah.
In the video, which you can watch below, Garcia can be seen down on one knee asking for the 33-year-old Australian’s hand in marriage, with the video ending with the couple kissing.
Taking to social media, a jubilant Garcia wrote: “She said yes!!!!!!. I’m so happy and motivated going into my fight now.
“Let’s gooooooo. Lets go for real. She’s my wife or future wifey but still very very happy.
“Everyone have a great day.”
Savannah, who has starred in more than 100 adult films, has shared posts alongside Garcia on the her Instagram page.
Garcia is father to three children, two daughters and a son.
He drew criticism when he announced his divorce to ex-wife Andrea Celina just hours after the birth of their son in January of this year.
Andrea is also the mother to one of the American’s daughters.
Earlier this year 
Garcia has also hit headlines recently for his alarming social media activity.
Last month he shared an alarming video on his pages which suggesting he died after having his “throat slit”.
While he shared a follow-up video saying he was okay, along with ex-wife Andrea sharing a worried post online, there was more trouble as he started sharing conspiracy theories online.
He shared a theory about the Bohemian Grove, a private community north of San Francisco and west of Santa Rosa, and reposted a video claiming he was held captive there.
His activity online has also seen him appear to claim there will be an earthquake on June 6th.
Garcia has also made calls to “free” controversial influencer Andrew Tate after he was arrested and released in Romania with a sexual assault warrant in the UK.

title: John O’Shea’s quality colt Schwarz finally delivers on potential in Hawkesbury Guineas to earn shot at Brisbane winter carnival
subtitle: Trainer John O’Shea and connections of Schwarz were rewarded for their patience as the talented colt scored an impressive win in the Group 3 Hawkesbury Guineas.
content:
Gun colt Schwarz showed off the top level talent trainer John O’Shea has long believed he possessed with a stunning all-the-way Group 3 victory at Hawkesbury on Saturday.
 have long held his son of Zoustar in high regard but has been forced to wait patiently for him to fulfil his potential on the track.
That day could be set to arrive this preparation as 
It had been a frustrating preparation until this point for O’Shea and his connections.
Schwarz had been narrowly beaten in the Listed Darby Munro to start this preparation before racing without luck when sixth in the Group 2 Arrowfield 3YO Sprint last month.
ð¤ Schwarz leads all the way in the G3 Hawkesbury Guineas, giving 
O’Shea and jockey 
“We absolutely trust him emphatically. He is a top class animal and he showed that today,” O’Shea said.
“He gave nothing else a chance and was very strong through the line.
“He has won three races leading but that’s just circumstances and I am sure in a fast run seven (furlong) he can box seat.”
The anticipated rain finally hit Hawkesbury in the lead up to the three-year-old feature and had set in as the field went out for the Guineas but Schwarz relished the conditions.
McDonald was able to make the most of barrier one to put Schwarz at the tip of the spear and the colt was a clear leader as the field went down the back.
Schwarz ($2.40 fav) quickly shook off the challenge General Salute at the top of the straight before showing an superb turn of speed to put a gap on his rivals.
The speedy colt cleared out late to score by one-and-three-quarter lengths from 
It was McDonald’s third Hawkesbury Guineas victory following the wins of Chautauqua (2014) and Military Zone (2019) and brought up a winning treble for the stand-alone card.
“He behaved himself beautifully and is just maturing all the time,” McDonald said.
“He is a beautiful colt and has the best action. He really glides across the ground.
“Once he got in that position, he was always going to be hard to beat.
“He has a great turn of foot and high cruising speed so has a lot going for him.”
A date with the Group 3 $300,000 Fred Best Classic (1400m) at Eagle Farm on June 1 will be Schwartz’s next target.
The three-year-old feature holds ballot exemption for the 
TAB shortened Schwarz in Stradbroke Handicap betting from $26 into $15 following his Guineas win.
“He is right on track for where we want to be which is in the Stradbroke in about a month’s time,” O’Shea said.
“He is in good order, will go to the Fred Best in about three weeks and hopefully make his way into the Stradbroke field.
“I would think (he needs to win the Fred Best). 
“The way the weight the race now, they used to give three-year-olds and advantage but don’t any longer so I would say it would be a necessity for him to win.”
Schwarz was purchased as part of a partnership between Rosemont-Victorian Alliance, Suman Hedge Bloodstock (FBAA) and David Redvers Bloodstock for $1,250,000 at the 2022 Gold Coast Yearling Sale.
That will seem like a small price to pay if Schwarz can snare a Group 1 this preparation and ensure himself a place at stud in the next few years.

title: Gavin Bedggood full of admiration for gutsy gelding Just Folk after dramatic win in Hawkesbury Gold Cup
subtitle: The expected rain failed to arrive but gutsy gelding Just Folk dug deep to win the Hawkesbury Gold Cup and book a place in The Big Dance in November.
content:
Just Folk did everything he could to get himself beaten but still found a way to win at Hawkesbury on Saturday.
In an action-packed finish to the Group 3 $250,000 Hawkesbury Gold Cup (1600m), Just Folk ran about in the straight, leaving jockey 
But the drama didn’t end there. Welwal’s rider, 
Then 
Just Folk hangs on to win a thrilling G3 Hawkesbury Gold Cup for 
Clark was treated back in the jockeys room and his back pain soon eased while McDonald felt there wasn’t sufficient grounds to lodge a protest.
This left Cranbourne’s 
Just Folk is regarded as a superior wet-tracker and all week, Bedggood had been on weather watch with heavy rain forecast for Hawkesbury.
But when Bedggood got to Hawkesbury on raceday, he was dismayed to find the track was rated a Good 4.
“I was shattered when I got to the track,” Bedggood said.
“Just Folk doesn’t need bottomless ground but he definitely appreciates the sting out of it.
“But he is a genuine horse and since we have had him, he hasn’t run a bad race.”
Just Folk ($7) gave former jumps jockey Bedggood one of his biggest wins as a trainer when he scored by a short half head from Detonator Jack ($3.50 favourite) with Welwal ($7) a half neck away third.
The Hawkesbury Cup win also qualifies Just Folk for the $3 million The Big Dance (1600m) at Royal Randwick on the first Tuesday in November.
Bedggood revealed he purchased Just Folk as a tried horse for $199,000 last year and in eight starts for the stable, the striking chestnut gelding has won two Group 3 races and more than $420,000 prizemoney.
“Just Folk has more than paid his way for us,” Bedggood said.
“Everyone will say we have bought a good, tried horse but he was rising seven and had plenty of racing so there was an element of risk to getting him.
“We targeted the Hawkesbury Cup third-up on the way to Queensland as his best runs are his third and fourth runs back from a spell.
“It’s great to pull off the plan and this win is right up there with the best I’ve had as a trainer.”
Rawiller, who has known Bedggood since the trainer was a jumps jockey, said Just Folk seemed to lose concentration when he ran past the Hawkesbury grandstand with the winning post still 100m away.
“Just Folk did everything he could to try and get beat, I have to be honest with you,” Rawiller said.
“When we went past the stand, he got a bit lost – like we all do! The reins were a bit slippery which didn’t help either.
“He ran about a bit but then he really attacked the line. He’s a tough horse.”
Bedggood said Just Folk could even back-up in the Hollindale Stakes at the Sunshine Coast next Saturday.
“He was able to win fourth-up last preparation on a seven-day back-up,” Bedggood said.
“So, all going well he will run in the Hollindale next week. The plan is to give him two runs up there and then we will try and set him for The Big Dance.”
Detonator Jack, ridden by Josh Parr, went wide on the turn and unleashed a powerful surge to just miss running down Just Folk.
Welwal seemed to strike trouble inside the final 200m but Charlie Duckworth, stable representative for trainer Chris Waller, said after viewing a replay of the finish with jockey James McDonald, they agreed the horse had sufficient room in the straight and decided there were no grounds to lodge an objection.
